vignette:
He hasn’t slept more than three hours in a night since the Fourth of July, though the fireworks aren’t really the problem. It’s the quiet that gets him—the way the house falls still around two in the morning, the way the streetlight through the blinds throws a pale grid across the bedroom wall. His wife, Sarah, lies beside him, her breathing even, and he envies that. He lies perfectly still, listening for something he can’t name, his jaw tight enough that his molars ache by dawn.

Tom is thirty-six, a tax consultant at a mid-size firm in a Midwest city. He keeps a framed CPA license on his desk and a coffee mug that says “Audit? I’d rather fight a war.” He bought it himself, years ago, when he still thought that kind of humor was okay. He doesn’t think so now.

The war was Iraq, 2007. He was a specialist in a logistics unit, tasked with convoy security. The event that broke the seam in his mind happened on a road south of Baghdad. An IED ripped through the lead vehicle. He remembers the smoke, the screaming, the smell of diesel and burnt rubber. He pulled a man from the wreckage—a private named Kowalski, nineteen years old, legs gone below the knee. Tom held a tourniquet on what was left while the medic worked. Kowalski lived, but Tom still sees his face in the instant the sound hit, the open mouth, the eyes that said this is real.

Back home, he told himself he was fine. He married Sarah six months after redeploying. They bought a house, adopted a dog. He went to work, filed extensions, calculated deductions, answered client calls about capital gains. He was good at it. Numbers don’t lie; they don’t scream.

But the numbers started to blur. He finds himself staring at a Schedule C for twenty minutes, the lines swimming, because somewhere in the back of his head he’s replaying that road, checking for tripwires in the median, scanning rooftops. In client meetings, he flinches when someone drops a binder on the floor. He apologizes, says the coffee is too strong. He’s stopped taking the highway to work—the overpasses make him feel trapped, and once, last winter, he pulled over on the shoulder because his heart was pounding so hard he couldn’t see straight. He told Sarah he had a migraine.

At night, the dreams come. Not every night, but enough. In the dream, he’s back in the Humvee, and the radio is static, and Kowalski is in the seat beside him, whole and grinning, and then the ground opens up and Tom is falling, falling, and he wakes with his fists clenched and the sheet soaked. Sarah has learned not to touch him when he wakes up. She waits until he says her name.

He’s irritable in ways that frighten him. Last week, a telemarketer called during dinner and he slammed the phone on the counter so hard the screen cracked. Sarah looked at him, not afraid, but tired. He saw her face and felt a shame that burned all the way down. He doesn’t talk about Iraq. When coworkers ask about his time in the service, he says “supply chain stuff” and changes the subject. He avoids the veterans’ group at the library. He avoids the news. He avoids anything that might trigger—but the triggers are everywhere. A car backfires and he’s on the floor of the garage before he knows what happened. A certain smell—grilled meat, or diesel—makes his stomach clench.

He hasn’t told Sarah about the PCL-5 he filled out in the waiting room. Score of seventy. He knows what that means—he’s seen the scoring guide on the psychologist’s clipboard. He’s here because his doctor insisted, because his blood pressure is through the roof, because Sarah said she couldn’t live with the man he’d become. So he sits in the chair, across from the therapist, and tells her about the sleepless nights and the client who complained that he seemed “distracted.” He doesn’t tell her about the moment last month when he found himself checking a restaurant’s exits six times before he could sit down. He doesn’t tell her that sometimes, when he looks at his wife, he feels so far away from her that he wonders if he’s already gone.

He glances at the clock on the wall. It’s eleven in the morning. He has three hours before his next appointment, a couple with a small business and a messy partnership return. He needs to focus. But the therapist is asking him about the Fourth of July, about the fireworks, about the quiet. And Tom realizes that somewhere inside, he’s still on that road, and the road hasn’t ended.
